scene-u01.name: Pattern Recognition Week 3 KP13 Logistic Regression (expert-first, English)

p01-logodds-title.name: p01-logodds-title
p01-logodds-title.text: A probability is confined to 0–1; as "log odds" it has no bounds and can be written as a linear score

p01-logodds-ctx.name: p01-logodds-ctx
p01-logodds-ctx.text: The odds $p/(1-p)$ compare occurring with not occurring; their logarithm is called the logit.

p01-logodds-src.name: p01-logodds-src
p01-logodds-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §1: $\ln\frac p{1-p}=z=b+\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$ is a modeling assumption and real data need not obey it; $p=0.2,0.5,0.8$ are this page's illustration.

p01-logodds-c0.name: p01-logodds-c0
p01-logodds-c0.text: A probability $p$ can only be between $0$ and $1$. Turned into the log odds $\ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}$, how are the values distributed?

p01-logodds-c1.name: p01-logodds-c1
p01-logodds-c1.text: The blue line is $\ln\dfrac p{1-p}$: it runs down without bound as $p$ nears $0$ and up without bound as $p$ nears $1$; at $p=0.5$ it is $0$.

p01-logodds-c2.name: p01-logodds-c2
p01-logodds-c2.text: Three points: $p=0.2$: odds $0.25$, log odds $-1.3863$; $p=0.5$: odds $1$, $0$; $p=0.8$: odds $4$, log odds $1.3863$.

p01-logodds-c3.name: p01-logodds-c3
p01-logodds-c3.text: This quantity can be positive or negative and has no bounds, so it suits a linear score $b+\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$. This is a statistical modeling assumption; real data need not fit it exactly.

p02-solve-title.name: p02-solve-title
p02-solve-title.text: Assume the log odds equal a linear score z: exponentiate and rearrange to get p = 1/(1+e^{−z})

p02-solve-ctx.name: p02-solve-ctx
p02-solve-ctx.text: Each step is algebra on the same modeling equation.

p02-solve-src.name: p02-solve-src
p02-solve-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §2; the $z=3$ numbers are the lecture §3 example, $e^{-3}=0.049787068$, $p=0.952574127$, recomputed by build_kp13_en.py.

p02-solve-c0.name: p02-solve-c0
p02-solve-c0.text: Known model: $\ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}=z=b+\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$. Solve for $p$: what shape does it have? What is its range?

p02-solve-c2.name: p02-solve-c2
p02-solve-c2.text: Step two: multiply both sides by $(1-p)$ and rearrange. $p=e^z(1-p)\ \Rightarrow\ p(1+e^z)=e^z$.

p02-solve-c4.name: p02-solve-c4
p02-solve-c4.text: A finite $z$ always gives $0<p<1$; only $z\to\pm\infty$ approaches the endpoints. Choosing $p=0.5$ as the threshold means $z=0$: the boundary is still a hyperplane in the current feature space, and the curvature of the probability curve does not by itself create a curved boundary.

p03-sigmoid-title.name: p03-sigmoid-title
p03-sigmoid-title.text: The sigmoid turns any score z into a probability between 0 and 1: z=0 gives 0.5, the two ends hug 0 and 1

p03-sigmoid-ctx.name: p03-sigmoid-ctx
p03-sigmoid-ctx.text: Lecture §3 example: $b=0,\ w=1.5$, so $z=1.5x$; the three test points $x=-2,\ 0,\ 2$ correspond to $z=-3,\ 0,\ 3$. The horizontal axis is the score $z$, not the original input $x$.

p03-sigmoid-src.name: p03-sigmoid-src
p03-sigmoid-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §3: $p(-3)=0.047426$, $p(0)=0.5$, $p(3)=0.952574$; in one dimension with $w\ne0$ the threshold is $x=-b/w$, and with $w=0$ the probability is the same everywhere.

p03-sigmoid-c0.name: p03-sigmoid-c0
p03-sigmoid-c0.text: As the score goes from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, how does the probability change? What does $z=0$ give? And $z=\pm3$?

p03-sigmoid-c1.name: p03-sigmoid-c1
p03-sigmoid-c1.text: The blue S-shaped curve $\sigma(z)=\dfrac1{1+e^{-z}}$: the left end hugs $0$, the right end hugs $1$ and never goes beyond (the red dashed lines are $0$ and $1$).

p03-sigmoid-c2.name: p03-sigmoid-c2
p03-sigmoid-c2.text: Green point: at $z=0$, $p=0.5$. Choosing $0.5$ as the threshold makes the boundary $z=0$, at $x=-b/w$ in one dimension.

p03-sigmoid-c3.name: p03-sigmoid-c3
p03-sigmoid-c3.text: Orange points: $z=-3$ ($x=-2$) $p=0.047426$; $z=3$ ($x=2$) $p=0.952574$. These are model probabilities, not measured accuracy.

p03-sigmoid-c4.name: p03-sigmoid-c4
p03-sigmoid-c4.text: If $w=0$ the probability is the same everywhere; for $w\neq0$ the boundary is still a hyperplane, and the curvature of the probability curve does not create a curved boundary.

p04-multiclass-title.name: p04-multiclass-title
p04-multiclass-title.text: Several classes: pick one class as the reference (score 0), exponentiate the other scores, then divide by the total

p04-multiclass-src.name: p04-multiclass-src
p04-multiclass-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §4 [supplementary example]: exponentials $2,3,1$, denominator $6$, probabilities $(1/3,1/2,1/6)$; changing the reference class does not change the probabilities, only the parameterization.

p04-multiclass-c0.name: p04-multiclass-c0
p04-multiclass-c0.text: Three scores $(\ln2,\ \ln3,\ 0)$: what do they look like after exponentiating? After dividing by the total, what are the three probabilities?

p04-multiclass-c1.name: p04-multiclass-c1
p04-multiclass-c1.text: The three add up to $6$. Dividing each by $6$ shrinks the total to $1$.

p04-multiclass-c3.name: p04-multiclass-c3
p04-multiclass-c3.text: Changing the reference class does not change the probabilities, only how the parameters are written. For $M=2$ this is the previous page's sigmoid.

p05-likelihood-title.name: p05-likelihood-title
p05-likelihood-title.text: Learning: maximize the product of correct-label probabilities: minimize the negative log-likelihood

p05-likelihood-ctx.name: p05-likelihood-ctx
p05-likelihood-ctx.text: For binary labels: $\mathcal L=-\sum_n[y_n\ln p_n+(1-y_n)\ln(1-p_n)]=\sum_n[\ln(1+e^{z_n})-y_nz_n]$. Plot the loss of one positive sample.

p05-likelihood-src.name: p05-likelihood-src
p05-likelihood-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §5 [supplementary example]: for a positive sample with $z=3$, $\ln(1+e^{-3})\approx0.048587$; with $z=-3$, $\ln(1+e^{3})\approx3.048587$; implementation uses `np.logaddexp(0, z) - y*z`.

p05-likelihood-c0.name: p05-likelihood-c0
p05-likelihood-c0.text: This sample's label is positive. The larger the score $z$, the smaller the loss $-\ln p=\ln(1+e^{-z})$. What do $z=3$ and $z=-3$ each pay?

p05-likelihood-c1.name: p05-likelihood-c1
p05-likelihood-c1.text: The blue curve $\ln(1+e^{-z})$: the more correct the prediction (larger $z$) the closer the loss to $0$; the more wrong and the more confident (smaller $z$), the loss grows almost linearly with $-z$.

p05-likelihood-c2.name: p05-likelihood-c2
p05-likelihood-c2.text: Green point: $z=3$, loss $\ln(1+e^{-3})=0.048587$. Correct and confident, it pays almost nothing.

p05-likelihood-c3.name: p05-likelihood-c3
p05-likelihood-c3.text: Red point: also a positive sample but $z=-3$, loss $\ln(1+e^{3})=3.048587$. Confidently wrong, it pays a lot.

p05-likelihood-c4.name: p05-likelihood-c4
p05-likelihood-c4.text: Programs use the stable form $\ln(1+e^z)-yz$ (log-sum-exp) to avoid huge exponentials; for multiclass first subtract the maximum score.

p06-lda-title.name: p06-lda-title
p06-lda-title.text: Versus LDA: same log-odds form, but the prior moves the threshold; assumptions and estimation differ

p06-lda-src.name: p06-lda-src
p06-lda-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §6 [supplementary example]: $z=2x+\ln(1/3)$, threshold $x=\ln3/2\approx0.549306$; if the prior is left out the threshold is wrongly $0$. Numbers recomputed by build_kp13_en.py.

p06-lda-c0.name: p06-lda-c0
p06-lda-c0.text: The two classes have means $\pm1$ and a shared variance $1$, but the positive class is only $25\%$. What does the posterior curve look like? Where is the $0.5$ threshold?

p06-lda-c1.name: p06-lda-c1
p06-lda-c1.text: Gray dashed: prior left out, $z=2x$, threshold at $x=0$. This is wrong when priors are unequal.

p06-lda-c2.name: p06-lda-c2
p06-lda-c2.text: Blue line: with the prior $\ln(1/3)=-1.0986$, $z=2x-1.0986$, threshold $x=\dfrac{\ln3}2=0.5493$. The positive class is rarer, so the threshold moves right.

p06-lda-c3.name: p06-lda-c3
p06-lda-c3.text: Same form does not mean same estimation: LDA assumes Gaussians with a shared covariance and estimates from means and covariances; logistic regression assumes only that the log odds are affine and maximizes the conditional likelihood directly. Having no Gaussian assumption does not guarantee beating LDA either.

p07-pitfalls-title.name: p07-pitfalls-title
p07-pitfalls-title.text: Three limits: no finite optimum if separable, valid ≠ accurate, no Gaussian ≠ better

p07-pitfalls-ctx.name: p07-pitfalls-ctx
p07-pitfalls-ctx.text: One-dimensional perfectly separable data: $x=-2,-1$ labeled $0$, $x=1,2$ labeled $1$; take $b=0$. As the weight $w$ grows, how does the negative log-likelihood $L(w)$ change?

p07-pitfalls-src.name: p07-pitfalls-src
p07-pitfalls-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §5 source note and §6: separable data's likelihood nears its supremum only as weights diverge; valid ≠ calibrated; $L(w)=2\ln(1+e^{-w})+2\ln(1+e^{-2w})$ is illustrative (build_kp13_en.py).

p07-pitfalls-c0.name: p07-pitfalls-c0
p07-pitfalls-c0.text: As $w$ grows, where does $L(w)$ go? Does it reach $0$?

p07-pitfalls-c1.name: p07-pitfalls-c1
p07-pitfalls-c1.text: The blue line $L(w)$ keeps falling and approaches $0$, but for every $w$ a larger $w$ is better still: there is no finite optimal weight.

p07-pitfalls-c3.name: p07-pitfalls-c3
p07-pitfalls-c3.text: A valid probability only guarantees falling in $[0,1]$ and normalizing; it does not guarantee a correct or calibrated model.

p07-pitfalls-c4.name: p07-pitfalls-c4
p07-pitfalls-c4.text: No Gaussian assumption does not guarantee beating LDA: logistic regression still assumes the log odds are affine in the current features.

p07-pitfalls-c5.name: p07-pitfalls-c5
p07-pitfalls-c5.text: Practice needs suitable constraints (such as regularization) and a stopping criterion.

p08-practice-title.name: p08-practice-title
p08-practice-title.text: Practice: b = $−2$, w = 0.5: the probability at x = 4? Where is the threshold at which the probability is 0.5?

p08-practice-ctx.name: p08-practice-ctx
p08-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: first find the score $z=b+wx$, then apply the sigmoid. The numbers are an abstract income indicator with no stated currency. Press Next when done.

p08-practice-src.name: p08-practice-src
p08-practice-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture practice; (c) is $x=8$ added by this deck; answer computed by build_kp13_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp13_en.py.

p08-practice-q.name: p08-practice-q
p08-practice-q.text: (a) The model probability at $x=4$? (b) The threshold $x$ where the probability is $0.5$? (c) (supplement) The probability at $x=8$?

p08-practice-a2.name: p08-practice-a2
p08-practice-a2.text: (b) $p=0.5\iff z=0\iff x=-b/w=4$. The same point as (a).

p09-summary-title.name: p09-summary-title
p09-summary-title.text: Summary: linear log odds give a valid probability; learn parameters by conditional likelihood

p09-summary-ctx.name: p09-summary-ctx
p09-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the sigmoid curve; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p09-summary-e0.name: p09-summary-e0
p09-summary-e0.text: The log odds $\ln\frac p{1-p}$ are unbounded and can be positive or negative, so we assume they equal a linear score $z=b+\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$

p09-summary-e1.name: p09-summary-e1
p09-summary-e1.text: Solving back gives $p=\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$; a finite $z$ always gives $0<p<1$; $z=0$ gives $0.5$, and the boundary is still a hyperplane

p09-summary-e2.name: p09-summary-e2
p09-summary-e2.text: Multiclass: pick a reference class, $p_i=e^{z_i}/(1+\sum_{j<M}e^{z_j})$; such as $(\ln2,\ln3,0)\to(1/3,1/2,1/6)$

p09-summary-e3.name: p09-summary-e3
p09-summary-e3.text: Learning parameters: maximize the conditional likelihood: minimize the binary cross entropy $\sum[\ln(1+e^{z})-yz]$; same form as LDA but different assumptions

p09-summary-e4.name: p09-summary-e4
p09-summary-e4.text: Limits: separable data has no finite optimal weights; a valid probability ≠ accurate. Next KP: choose the hyperplane by maximum margin

p06-gauss-title.text: Gaussians with a shared covariance: the log ratio is exactly a linear function of $\mathbf x$
p06-gauss-title.name: p06-gauss-title

p06-gauss-ctx.text: The LDA assumption: each class has Gaussian features $N(\mathbf m_i,\Sigma)$ with one shared covariance $\Sigma$; the class prior is $\pi_i$. Bayes rule gives the log ratio of the two posteriors.
p06-gauss-ctx.name: p06-gauss-ctx

p06-gauss-src.text: Source: KP13 lecture §6 (LDA log ratio); the one-dimensional example uses the same setup as the next page (means $\pm1$, variance $1$, priors $1/4$ and $3/4$), recomputed independently. Added page: the original deck gave only the one-dimensional result, restored the general derivation from the lecture.
p06-gauss-src.name: p06-gauss-src

p06-gauss-tl.text: Blue: $\pi_1\cdot N(x;1,1)$ with $\pi_1=1/4$; orange: $\pi_2\cdot N(x;-1,1)$ with $\pi_2=3/4$
p06-gauss-tl.name: p06-gauss-tl

p06-gauss-c0.text: $\ln\dfrac{P(\omega_1\mid\mathbf x)}{P(\omega_2\mid\mathbf x)}=\ln\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}-\tfrac12(\mathbf x-\mathbf m_1)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\mathbf m_1)+\tfrac12(\mathbf x-\mathbf m_2)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\mathbf m_2)$: the prior ratio plus the log ratio of the two Gaussian densities (the common constant cancels).
p06-gauss-c0.name: p06-gauss-c0

p06-gauss-c1.text: Expand the two quadratics: the term $\mathbf x^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x$ is the same on both sides because $\Sigma$ is shared, so it cancels. Only the linear term in $\mathbf x$ and constants remain.
p06-gauss-c1.name: p06-gauss-c1

p06-gauss-c2.text: $\ln\dfrac{P(\omega_1\mid\mathbf x)}{P(\omega_2\mid\mathbf x)}=\ln\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}+\tfrac12\left(\mathbf m_2^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf m_2-\mathbf m_1^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf m_1\right)+(\mathbf m_1-\mathbf m_2)^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x$: an affine function of $\mathbf x$, the same form assumed by logistic regression.
p06-gauss-c2.name: p06-gauss-c2

p06-gauss-c3.text: One-dimensional example: $m_1=1$, $m_2=-1$, $\Sigma=1$, $\pi_1=\tfrac14$, $\pi_2=\tfrac34$. The constant is $\ln\tfrac13+\tfrac12(1-1)=-1.0986$ and the slope is $(1-(-1))/1=2$, so $z=2x-1.0986$; the two weighted densities cross at $x=\tfrac{\ln3}{2}=0.5493$ (red line), where $z=0$.
p06-gauss-c3.name: p06-gauss-c3

p06-gauss-c4.text: The same form does not mean the same estimate: LDA estimates from means and covariance, while logistic regression maximizes the conditional likelihood directly. With unequal priors the constant $\ln(\pi_1/\pi_2)$ moves the threshold away from $0$ (next page).
p06-gauss-c4.name: p06-gauss-c4

p06-gauss-cue0.text: First, the log ratio given by Bayes rule.
p06-gauss-cue0.name: p06-gauss-cue0

p06-gauss-cue1.text: See the blue card: the quadratic term cancels.
p06-gauss-cue1.name: p06-gauss-cue1

p06-gauss-cue2.text: See the green card: an affine function remains.
p06-gauss-cue2.name: p06-gauss-cue2

p06-gauss-cue3.text: See the two curves: the one-dimensional example and the crossing.
p06-gauss-cue3.name: p06-gauss-cue3
